claims.text: Protective passivating oxide films are key to the corrosion resistance of high-entropy alloys.
Mechanical wear disrupts the passive film during tribo-corrosion.
Passive-film disruption exposes fresh, more reactive alloy surfaces.
Freshly exposed alloy surfaces corrode more rapidly than film-covered surfaces.
Localized corrosion compromises surface integrity and accelerates wear.
Coupled degradation is governed by synergy between mechanical film removal and enhanced corrosion.
Balanced inclusion of oxide-forming elements such as Cr and Al produces a continuous protective oxide film.
Corrosion-induced surface weakening makes the alloy more susceptible to further mechanical damage.
Wear and corrosion establish a positive feedback loop.
Total degradation under tribo-corrosion will exceed that predicted by adding the independent effects of wear and corrosion.
The wear component will be amplified by passive-film removal.
Corrosion rates in worn areas will exceed the corrosion rate under static immersion.
Under static immersion, the passive film remains largely intact and provides corrosion resistance.
The prediction should hold for high-entropy alloys that form and maintain robust passive films under static conditions.
The prediction may fail for alloys that do not develop stable passive films.
The prediction may fail where corrosive attack is minimal regardless of wear.
The magnitude of wear-corrosion synergy varies with alloy composition, passive-film stability, pH, and chloride concentration.

contradictions.description: The predicted synergy is defined as degradation exceeding the sum of independent wear and corrosion effects, but the proposed comparison includes only tribo-corrosion and static corrosion. It lacks a wear-only control, so it cannot isolate or test the claimed super-additive interaction or determine whether the wear component is amplified.
